Shu Chengqi saw Laozi, who remained indifferent and did not respond. The next day, Shu Chengqi visited again and said, "Formerly, I had criticisms leveled against you. Now, my heart is corrected and at peace. Why was this?"

Laozi replied, "Those people endowed with cleverness and knowledge, who call themselves sages and holy ones, I consider myself to have freed myself from such concerns. Formerly, when you called me 'ox,' I accepted the name 'ox.' When you called me 'horse,' I accepted the name 'horse.' If there is a reality, people attach names to it. To refuse the name is to invite further calamity. My acceptance is simply to wear what I naturally wear; I do not wear it because I am adhering to an external code of conduct."

Shu Chengqi stepped back, avoiding his own shadow, walking sideways in humility.

Zi Sang Pi reproached him: "The true sage does not hear [of worldly praise]; why do you rejoice?" Confucius said, "Well said! He has discarded flowery rhetoric; he has left behind his disciples and fled to the great marshes. He wears coarse animal hair for clothing, eats wild nuts, <margin>not cherishing delicacies</margin>, and does not stir up the heart of differentiation, <margin>thus not disturbing the flocks of birds and beasts</margin>. When he enters among beasts, they do not break their ranks; when he enters among birds, they do not scatter their formations. Birds and beasts are not distressed by him, let alone humans."

Confucius asked Zi Sang Pi: "I was driven out twice from Lu, had trees cut down in Song, my footprints were erased in Wei, I faced starvation in Shang, and was besieged between Chen and Cai. I have suffered these several calamities. My close friends grew distant, and my companions scattered. Why is this so?"

<margin><term>Su</term> <gloss>Su Shi’s commentary</gloss></margin> To pursue study without knowing [the Dao] is to let knowledge and perception accumulate day by day, without a unifying principle. This inevitably becomes a burden. Confucius said, “Hear much, select the good, and follow it; see much, and remember it. This is next to true knowledge.” If one were to know the Way in a single day, one would see that falsehood has no part in it. By discarding falsehood, one returns to true nature. This is called “diminishing.” Confucius asked Zigong, “Do you think I am a man of much learning who memorizes things?” Zigong said, “Yes, isn’t that so?” Confucius replied, “No. I unify them all with a single thread.” When the mind forgets distinctions to restore purity, there is no such thing as diminishment. Yet if false notions remain, even this pure mind cannot fully restore nature. Only when both the act of diminishing and the object diminished are forgotten does the mind become purely restored. Then one can act without departing from non-action. Everyone desires to take over the world, seeking only rational order. Therefore, when they create situations, their intentions are visible outwardly, and people reject them. Thus, success is difficult to achieve. The sage acts without action, therefore has no troubled affairs. His mind is revealed outwardly, yet people feel at peace. Although he does not seek to manage the world’s affairs, those affairs naturally find order and peace through him.

<margin><term>Lü</term> <gloss>Lü Dajin’s commentary</gloss></margin> Those who study but have not heard the Way must broaden their search, hence it is called “increasing.” Those who practice the Way and have already heard it must engage in non-action, hence it is called “diminishing.” Further diminishing implies still being entangled in action. Only when even the concept of diminishing is discarded does one reach non-action. Non-action means being silent and unmoving. It also means responding and instantly connecting with all causes in the world. Non-action reaching its ultimate state—this is what is meant by scriptural learning. Freedom from worry is called divine/mysterious. The manner of the mysterious is the Dao itself. When one reaches the most mysterious, who could rival this? From this we see that taking over the world always begins with non-action. Once action arises, it is insufficient to truly take over the world. This is clear.

<column-break/>

<margin><term>Huang Maocai</term> <gloss>Huang Maocai’s commentary</gloss></margin> One must know nothing [preferentially] before one can speak of learning; therefore, learning requires daily increase. One must do nothing [selfishly] before one can speak of the Way; therefore, the Way requires daily diminution. However, increasing can be pursued actively, while diminishing is difficult to force. Only the perfectly enlightened can suddenly break free and drop all attachments, reaching the place of non-action. Thus, they can do everything, and their applications never exhaust. Applied to the world, they are abundantly sufficient.

<margin><term>Xi Zhai</term> <gloss>The Pavilion of Rest’s commentary</gloss></margin> Studying serves to acquire knowledge, hence it increases daily. Practicing the Way serves to remove falsehood, hence it diminishes daily. If knowledge is not extreme, diminution is incomplete. Thus, daily increase provides the ground for daily diminution. If one diminishes further and further, removing falsehood until truth is complete, one reaches non-action. When one reaches non-action, everything previously done was never truly done [in the egoic sense]. This is difficult to discuss merely in terms of increase and decrease. When non-action is fully realized, even the multiplicity of the world is unified. If one creates situations out of events, there will be no leisure. Even one single object previously stuck in entanglement and error—if that is hard to manage, how much more so the multitude of the world?

The sage has no constant mind; he takes the minds of the people as his own. He treats the good with goodness; he treats the bad with goodness too—thus virtue becomes perfectly good. He trusts the trustworthy; he trusts the untrustworthy too—thus trust becomes perfectly trusted. The sage dwells in the world with a hazy, undifferentiated demeanor, blurring the hearts of the people. All the people focus their eyes and ears [on the sage], but the sage...

The Duke of Zhou said: "When the birds are about to fly, their chirping is mournful; when the beasts are about to die, their bellowing is sorrowful. What is captured easily is hard to let go of; what is obtained recently is hard to forget. I have heard that the great vessel takes long to complete, and the great sound is late to resonate." Confucius said: "If one were a perfect man, what more could there be? If one were wise, what more could one say?" Yan Hui asked: "What does 'perfect man' mean?" Confucius said: "In ancient times, those who understood the Dao did not distinguish between themselves and others. Now, since you and I have already distinguished ourselves from each other, how can we talk about the perfect man? Moreover, if heaven gives life to me and earth forms my body, I am but a lump of flesh. Why should I worry about whether or not I am accepted by others? The sages consider it a burden to be alive, but I do not see why. If I were to become a left wheel of a cart, would that be bad? If I were to become a right wheel, would that be good? To take whatever comes as natural is to avoid sorrow; to accept change with equanimity is to avoid fear. Therefore, the ancients said: 'One’s place is fixed; one’s fate is determined.' How then can I worry about whether or not I am accepted by others?"

Confucius sent Zigong to invite the Master of Shang. The Master of Shang said: "Why does the Master come?" Confucius said: "I hear that the Master has attained the Dao. I wish to pay my respects." The Master of Shang said: "How do you know that I have attained the Dao?" Confucius said: "I know that you have attained the Dao because you do not seek to attain it." The Master of Shang said: "How do you know that you do not speak of it?" Confucius said: "I know that I do not speak of it because I do not speak of it." The Master of Shang said: "How do you know that you do not speak of it?" Confucius said: "I know that I do not speak of it because I do not speak of it."

Zilu asked to go and summon him. Confucius said: "Enough! He knows that I know him. He knows that I am going to Chu. He thinks that I will certainly make the King of Chu summon him. He considers me a flattering person. If this is so, he will be ashamed to hear the words of a flattering person, let alone see his face. Why should I bother to keep him?" Zilu went to look for him, but his house was empty.

The Lord of Changwu asked Zimu: "When you govern, do not be careless. When you rule the people, do not be fragmented. Once, I saw a small insect on a leaf. It had two wings and four legs. It was very beautiful. But when the wind blew, it fell off the leaf and died. I thought to myself: 'This is because it did not know how to hold on.' So I said to the leaf: 'Hold on tightly.' The leaf said: 'I cannot hold on tightly because I am small.' I said: 'Then why did you grow so big?' The leaf said: 'Because the soil was rich and the roots were strong.' I said: 'Then why did you fall off?' The leaf said: 'Because the wind was strong.' I said: 'Then why did the wind blow so strongly?' The leaf said: 'Because the sky was angry.' I said: 'Then why was the sky angry?' The leaf said: 'Because I did not know how to hold on.'"

# Wine and the Observation of Character

Observe their conduct through wine; observe their true nature when they are mixed with others. When all nine signs of character are present, even an unworthy person can be recognized.

Consider Zheng Kaofu. At his first appointment as a scholar-official, he bowed low; at his second appointment as a higher official, he bent further; at his third appointment, he stooped so deeply that he had to crawl along the wall to avoid blocking the path. Who would dare not to conform to such propriety? Thus it was with Zheng Kaofu’s lineage. Who would not take this as a model to follow?

The arrogant man, however, stands upright on his chariot; the haughty man lifts his carriage high; the proud man calls his elders by name. Yet Xu You renounced virtue itself. To act with deliberate intent toward virtue is to become its thief. If one labors to show virtue in the blink of an eye or the twitch of an eyelid, virtue becomes distorted.

Without doubt, animals lack a human heart; yet even if they possess an animal heart, their appearance often makes them seem familiar or approachable. Conversely, it is said that creatures with horns, fangs, and claws, which fly looking upward or crawl on the ground, are called birds and beasts; yet they may well possess a human heart. Even if humans have a human heart, their distinct appearance can cause others to feel distant or estranged.

Paoxi (Fuxi), Nüwa, Shennong, and the descendants of Xia Hou all had bodies resembling snakes and faces of humans, or ox heads and tiger noses. These forms were unlike those of ordinary people, yet these figures possessed the virtue of great sages. In contrast, Jie of Xia, Zhou of Yin (Shang), Huan of Lu, and Mu of Chu, though their physical features—seven openings and overall shape—were identical to those of humans, harbored the hearts of birds and beasts. Yet the masses cling to a single outward form in their quest for supreme wisdom, a goal that remains elusive.

The Yellow Emperor fought against the Flame Emperor in the wilderness of Banquan. He led bears, bison, wolves, leopards, Pixiu, and tigers as his vanguard, while carving eagles, hawks, falcons, and kites onto his banners. This was using force to command birds and beasts.

# Xunzi: Correct Discourses

In ancient times, the Son of Heaven had a thousand officials, and feudal lords had a hundred. With this structure, if commands were enforced throughout the states of Xia (Huaxia), they were called "Kings" (Wang). If, with this smaller body of officials, commands were enforced within their own territories—even if those states were unstable—they would not lose their office or perish entirely. This is what we call "Lords" (Jun).

The sons of Sage Kings, and the successors who hold the mandate under Heaven, are the ancestral clans of all under Heaven. Yet if they lack talent and do not conform to the mean (justice/propriety), internally the common people will hate them, and externally the feudal lords will rebel against them. Those nearby will refuse unity within the territory; those far away will ignore their commands. Commands will not be enforced within their borders. At worst, feudal lords will encroach upon and attack them. In such a case, although the state has not yet officially collapsed, I say they have lost the Mandate of Heaven.

When a Sage King dies and no successor holds the register of authority, the weak and incompetent cannot maintain the connection <note>原文「罷」，音皮，意為柔弱、不能勝任</note> with the world. With no ruler over all under Heaven, if among the feudal lords there is one whose virtue is clear and whose prestige is accumulated, so that the people everywhere wish to make him their ruler and teacher, but a tyrannical state alone acts arrogantly <note>暴國指桀紂之類；獨侈言放縱；安猶則也</note>, how can he destroy it? He must surely avoid harming innocent people. To punish the tyrant of a violent state is like punishing a solitary man <note>獨夫：天下皆無助之者，若一夫然也</note>. If it is thus, then it can be said that he could properly use all under Heaven. To be able to use all under Heaven is to be called a "King" (Wang).

Tang and Wu did not seize all under Heaven by force. They cultivated the Way and practiced righteousness. They shared the benefits that all under Heaven desired and removed the harms that all under Heaven detested. Thus, all under Heaven turned to them. Jie and Zhou did not abandon all under Heaven; rather, they reversed the virtue of Yu, Tang, and Wu. They confused the distinctions of ritual and righteousness, acting like beasts. They accumulated their wickedness and consolidated their cruelty <note>下疑為「残」或類似字，意為殘忍</note>.

<summary>This passage from Xunzi's "Correct Discourses" defines the legitimacy of rule through the effective enforcement of commands and the moral character of the ruler. It contrasts the stable authority of ancient sage-kings with the inevitable loss of power by incompetent successors, arguing that true kingship (like that of Tang and Wu) arises from shared benefit and righteousness rather than force, while tyrants (Jie and Zhou) lose their mandate by reversing virtue and acting beastly.</summary>

# Diamond Sutra (Vol 3)

Those who perceive form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and phenomena are called Stream-Enterers.

What do you think? Can they think to themselves, "I have attained the fruit of the Stream-Enterer?"

Subhuti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this so? The term 'Stream-Enterer' implies a one-way entry, yet in reality there is no entering or going. Therefore, it is called Stream-Enterer."

Subhuti, what do you think? Can a Once-Returner think to himself, "I have attained the fruit of the Once-Returner"?

Subhuti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this so? Because the term 'Once-Returner' suggests returning, yet in reality there is no returning. Therefore, it is called Once-Returner."

Subhuti, what do you think? Can a Non-Returner think to himself, "I have attained the fruit of the Non-Returner"?

Subhuti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this so? Because the term 'Non-Returner' suggests not returning, yet in reality there is no non-returning. Therefore, it is called Non-Returner."

<summary>This passage from the Diamond Sutra deconstructs the spiritual attainments of the first three stages of enlightenment—Stream-Enterer, Once-Returner, and Non-Returner—by emphasizing that true realization involves no sense of self-attainment or movement between states.</summary>

### Chapter 7: On No Attainment and No Teaching

Subhuti! What do you think? Has the Tathagata attained the supreme perfect enlightenment <note>original: Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi</note>? Does the Tathagata have any specific teachings to give?

Subhuti replied: According to my understanding of what the Buddha has taught, there is no fixed or definite dharma called "supreme perfect enlightenment," nor is there any fixed dharma that the Tathagata teaches. Why is this? Because all teachings given by the Tathagata cannot be grasped, cannot be expressed in words; they are neither a dharma nor a non-dharma. The reason for this is that all sages and saints differ from one another only because of their relationship with the unconditioned <note>original: Asamskrta</note> reality.

Daiyu laughed and said, "If you wish to learn to compose poetry, you must take me as your teacher. Although I am not fully proficient, I can certainly teach you the basics." Xiangling laughed and said, "If it is really like that, I will take you as my teacher. You must not grow tired of me." Daiyu said, "What difficulty could there be worth learning? It is merely a matter of structure: introduction, elucidation, transition, and conclusion. The middle section requires two parallel couplets: level tones (ping) correspond to oblique tones (ze); abstract concepts correspond to concrete ones, and concrete ones to abstract ones. Xiangling laughed and said, "No wonder I often sneak old poetry books to read a few verses at a time. Sometimes the couplets are extremely well-matched, and sometimes they are not. Xiangling said, "I simply adore Lu You’s line, 'Heavy curtains unrolled retain fragrance for long; an ancient inkstone slightly hollowed gathers more ink.' It feels so vivid and interesting!" Take it and carefully study one hundred of his five-character regulated verses until you understand them thoroughly. Afterward, read one hundred and twenty seven-character regulated verses by Du Fu. Next, read one or two hundred seven-character quatrains by Li Bai. With these three masters as your foundation, you can then glance at poets like Tao Yuanming, Ying Bi, Liu Yuxi, Xie Lingyun, Ruan Ji, Yu Xin, and Bao Zhao. Hearing this, Xiangling laughed and said, "In that case, good sister, please give me that book. I will take it back and read a few verses at night; that will be beneficial." Daiyu asked, "Have you grasped some of their essence?" Xiangling laughed and said, "I think I have gained some understanding, though I do not know if it is correct. Let me tell you about it."

The jing and yong pendants are removed, not going around to see the ruler. Kang Hou passes away; therefore, the poet sighs and laments this. This is the Lu School’s interpretation, which differs from the Mao School.

Ouyang Xiu states that the Qi, Lu, and Han schools all consider this a poem lamenting the decline of governance under King Kang. The *Prehistory Han History*, in the biography of Du Qin, records: "The jing and yong pendants ring late at night; 'Guan Ju' expresses a sigh." Zhang Yan comments: "This is the Lu School’s view." The edict of Emperor Ming of the Later Han states: "In ancient times, when the gatekeepers failed in their duty, 'Guan Ju' criticized the age." Xue Qiong, in his annotations on the Han School's *Xiaojing Zhangju*, explains: "When the sovereign leaves court, there are proper limits for concubines to present themselves. Watchmen beat drums at the gatehouse (Yingmen), and drummers on the tower sound alarms as people enter the hall. Now, because the inner palace has succumbed to lust, they chant 'Guan Ju,' describing the virtuous maiden to criticize the times."

Lü Zuqian observes that the Lu, Qi, Han, and Mao schools have different readings and interpretations. Since the first poem of the "Proper Odes" (*Guan Ju*) is treated by the three earlier schools (Lu, Qi, Han) as a criticism, one can infer how they viewed the rest. Wang Yinglin cites Shi Long Xue, who asserts that interpreting "Guan Ju" as a critique is correct. Some argue that those who composed the poem did so with an intent of "mourning without being destructive," but this cannot be known for certain. However, the *Rites of Ceremony* indicates that "Guan Ju" was used as local music for village gatherings and also as chamber music. This suggests that the poem existed during the time of the Duke of Zhou’s creations.

Purple Gromwell (Lithospermum)

Purple Gromwell is also known by the names Purple Cinnabar, Purple Hibiscus, Zi Xu, and Miao.

Er Ya states: "Miao" refers to Purple Gromwell.

One name for it is Earth Blood; another is Crow’s Beak Grass. It grows in the valleys of Dangshan, Xinye in Nanyang, and regions of Chu. Its seedlings resemble orchids, with a fragrance, red nodes, and green stems. In the second lunar month, it blooms with purple-and-white flowers. The fruit is also white. In autumn, the root turns purple and can be used to dye fabric purple. It has a sweet taste, cold nature, and is non-toxic.

*Materia Naturalis* records that on the southern slope of Pingshan, the purple gromwell is particularly fine.

*Guang Zhi* notes that purple gromwell from Longxi is the finest grade.

*Qimin Yaoshu* suggests that yellow and soft soils are excellent for cultivation; green sandy soil is also good. Plowing under millet or broomcorn fields yields large harvests.
